paper_title: ReLift: Dense 3D Tracking as Lifted Trajectory Repair

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Dense 3D point trajectories describe how scene content moves through space over time, and are key in downstream tasks such as manipulation policy learning, dynamic scene reconstruction, sensor simulation, and motion-controlled video generation (Chen et al., 2025; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2025; Borreda et al., 2026; Singer et al., 2026). Recovering them from 1 monocular video is usually posed as single learning problem: one feed-forward network is trained end to end to output 3D tracks. Such network has to learn three things at once: finding correspondence across frames, recovering the geometry of the scene, and inferring motion behind occlusions. However, pretrained models already excel at two of these tasks. Dedicated 2D trackers establish strong correspondences (Harley et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2026) and can exceed the image-plane accuracy of projected 3D predictions (Appendix C.4), while geometry models provide depth and cameras learned from scalable geometric supervision without requiring annotated dynamic 4D trajectories (Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). This motivates focusing the scarce 4D supervision on what remains: repairing errors in the combined estimates and completing occluded motion. We therefore introduce ReLift, which combines strong 2D correspondences and pretrained scene geometry for dense 3D tracking. We take the viewing ray of each point from 2D tracker and its range along that ray from depth model, and lift the two into 3D trajectory we call the lift. Since occluded tracks sample the occluders depth, we discard predictions flagged as occluded and initialize missing positions by interpolation. Even before learned correction, these initialized lifts can match or exceed the mean accuracy of learned 3D trackers using the same geometry (Tables 1 and 2). However, these lifts still lack observations during occlusion and suffer from jumps at depth boundaries and jitter from per-frame depth fluctuations. These failures can produce severe trajectory discontinuities and leave hidden motion unresolved. We recast dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. compact learned corrector preserves reliable observations while repairing corrupted positions and recovering missing motion. Alternating attention along and across tracks shares temporal and spatial evidence, while processing track groups independently keeps dense feed-forward correction efficient. natural training strategy is to run pretrained tracking and geometry models on synthetic videos with ground-truth 3D trajectories, then train the corrector to recover those trajectories from the resulting lifts. However, this ties the training inputs to the errors of the chosen estimators. We avoid this by training without ever running tracker, depth model, or renderer. We model the geometric effects of lifting failures directly as randomized corruptions of clean 3D trajectories from PointOdyssey (Zheng et al., 2023), producing simulated lifts from which we train network to recover the clean trajectories. Training uses geometric annotations without images or provider predictions, concentrating supervision on learning motion priors for trajectory repair and completion (Sec. 3.4). Our ablation supports this choice: training on simulated lifts improves accuracy over training on lifts generated by AllTracker and Depth Anything 3 (Sec. 4.4). Training on simulated lifts supports transfer across providers. We evaluate the same ReLift corrector without retraining with AllTracker (Harley et al., 2025) or CoWTracker (Lai et al., 2026), each paired with depth and camera estimates from Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025), VGGT-Ω (Wang et al., 2026), or 4RC (Luo et al., 2026). Correction improves all six lifts  (Fig. 3)  . Moreover, using the same depth and camera estimates as 4RC, our 2D tracking and correction pipeline achieves higher mean tracking accuracy than 4RCs trajectory predictions  (Table 1)  . Our contributions can be summarized as follows: strong lifting baseline. We show that pretrained 2D tracks lifted with estimated geometry and simple gap initialization can match or exceed dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework for dense monocular 3D tracking that combines pretrained 2D motion and 3D geometry through learned trajectory repair and completion. provider-agnostic training strategy based on randomized geometric corruptions of synthetic trajectories, without running tracking or geometry models during training. The same weights transfer across evaluated providers without retraining, allowing the framework to incorporate future advances in either component. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art mean dense 3D tracking accuracy on WorldTrack, with faster configurations retaining competitive accuracy at substantially lower runtime than comparably accurate 3D trackers.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Dynamic 3D reconstruction from monocular video. Classical non-rigid structure-from-motion methods recover time-varying 3D structure from image correspondences using local rigidity and low-rank constraints to reduce monocular ambiguity (Bregler et al., 2000; Akhter et al., 2008; Taylor et al., 2010; Dai et al., 2014). Modern per-video optimization methods combine image evidence with depth, tracking, and deformation priors (Zhang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). Shape of Motion (Wang et al., 2025b) and MoSca (Lei et al., 2024) combine pretrained depth and tracking cues with structured motion representations for reconstruction and rendering. These cues provide the initialization that rendering-based optimization needs, since photometric gradients vanish when rendered and observed content do not overlap (Cohen Rimon et al., 2026). Uni4D (Yao et al., 2025) and TrackingWorld (Lu et al., 2025) optimize camera poses and dense 3D trajectories from pretrained depth, tracking and segmentation models, or from densified 2D tracks. These methods demonstrate the strength of combining 2D motion with 3D geometry, but require lengthy per-scene optimization; we pursue this combination with feed-forward model. Feed-forward 3D geometry models. DUSt3R and MASt3R predict geometry and correspondences from image pairs (Wang et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024), while VGGT, VGGT-Ω, and Depth Anything 3 extend geometry estimation to multiple views (Wang et al., 2025a; 2026; Lin et al., 2025). MonST3R adapts point-map prediction to dynamic scenes and aligns predictions across video (Zhang et al., 2025b); St4RTrack and Dynamic Point Maps also represent motion and correspondences (Feng et al., 2025; Sucar et al., 2025), with V-DPM extending pairwise dynamic point maps to video (Sucar et al., 2026). Geometry and tracking capabilities thus overlap. In our pipeline, frozen geometry models supply depth and cameras, while 2D trackers establish point identities across frames. 2D tracking. 2D tracking follows the image projections of scene points over time. CoTracker jointly tracks multiple points (Karaev et al., 2024), while AllTracker and CoWTracker extend tracking to every reference-frame pixel (Harley et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2026). Per-video self-supervision also yields strong correspondences without ground-truth annotations for the input video: DINOTracker adapts pretrained image features (Tumanyan et al., 2024), while OmniMotion optimizes globally consistent tracks (Wang et al., 2023). These approaches show that correspondence estimation can exploit real-video evidence without annotated 3D motion, motivating its use as separate component. Our comparison supports reusing strong 2D correspondences: native CoWTracker surpasses the evaluated 3D methods in image-space accuracy (Appendix C.4). Established tracks also provide useful representation for recovering dynamic 3D structure. TracksTo4D reconstructs geometry and motion from 2D tracks using feed-forward, low-rank formulation without 3D supervision (Kasten et al., 2024). Seurat learns depth changes from 2D trajectories and combines them with pretrained depth estimates (Cho et al., 2025). Building on these precedents, ReLift starts from tracks already lifted with pretrained depth and cameras, and learns 3D residuals to repair corrupted observations and complete missing motion. Dense feed-forward 3D tracking. Feed-forward 3D trackers estimate trajectories from video, either jointly predicting geometry and motion or conditioning on externally supplied depth. DELTA and DELTAv2 predict dense long-range 3D tracks using video and depth inputs (Ngo et al., 2025b;a), while SpatialTrackerV2 jointly estimates geometry, camera motion, and point motion (Xiao et al., 2025). Trace Anything, Track4World, and 4RC predict dense trajectories or queryable geometry and motion (Liu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026). TrackCraft3R repurposes pretrained video-diffusion models for dense 3D tracking (Nam et al., 2026); MotionCrafter uses video generative priors for geometry and scene flow (Zhu et al., 2026). Available 3D motion supervision includes complete synthetic trajectories from PointOdyssey (Zheng et al., 2023) and trajectories reconstructed from real stereo videos in Stereo4D (Jin et al., 2025). We use PointOdyssey to learn repair and completion of lifted trajectories. Under matched geometry, these lifts already rival dedicated 3D trackers, and correction further improves them (Sec. 4.2).

sections.content: Given monocular video, we recover dense 3D trajectories in the camera coordinates of the reference frame I0. Frozen pretrained models supply 2D tracks, depth and camera estimates, which we combine into lifted trajectories (Sec. 3.1). The lift is accurate where tracking and depth are reliable. 3 Figure 2: Inference pipeline of ReLift. The output head predicts frame-level XYZ residuals, which are added to the initialized trajectories. We train the corrector on simulated lifts from clean trajectory annotations (Sec. 3.4). We use predicted visibility to mask observations, leaving gaps to complete. Retained observations may still be corrupted by missed occlusions, depth errors or tracking drift, and therefore require repair. Our corrector model uses positions, viewing rays and availability masks (Sec. 3.2). We hypothesize that temporal inconsistencies and disagreements between tracks provide cues for repair, while observations before and after gaps, together with related motion, can guide completion. We therefore use alternating attention along and across tracks to aggregate these cues and predict 3D residual corrections (Sec. 3.3). Temporal chunking and batched track groups enable efficient feed-forward correction over all reference pixels  (Fig. 2)  . No method receives ground-truth intrinsics (Appendices and B.2). 4.2 QUANTITATIVE RESULTS Accuracy. Our method achieves state-of-the-art mean APD3D on all and dynamic points with CoWTracker and 4RC geometry  (Table 1)  . It is particularly strong on the real-world datasets ADT and PS, where our variants lead both metrics. All six configurations share one trained corrector: for both trackers, mean accuracy increases from DA3 to VGGT-Ω to 4RC geometry, demonstrating gains from swapping geometry providers without retraining. Combining 2D motion and 3D geometry. To test the decomposition introduced in Sec. 1, we compare methods with the same geometry inputs. Even before correction, CoWTracker lifts with initialized gaps and VGGT-Ω geometry reach 84.9 mean all-point APD3D (Table 2, first row), compared with 83.9 for TrackCraft3R and 81.1 for DELTAv2 using the same geometry  (Table 1)  . After correction, our method outperforms both in every APD3D column of Table 1. Given 4RCs own geometry, our CoWTracker variant improves on 4RCs mean accuracy by 2.1 (All) and 5.4 (Dyn) points, demonstrating the advantage of our pipeline with geometry held fixed. On Kubric, our DA3 and VGGT-Ω variants trail 4RC but lead methods sharing their geometry on all-point APD3D; with 4RC geometry, ours outperform 4RC on dynamic points (Appendix C.1). Gains from trajectory repair and completion. Figure 3 measures what correction adds to the initialized lift (Sec. 3.2). Using 4RC geometry requires more time but delivers our highest mean accuracy. In spin, our trajectories form coherent arcs, while TrackCraft3R produces scattered paths. Our tracks follow the car through shadow-induced appearance changes in car-shadow and recover the dogs head after occlusion in libby, where competing predictions stop short. Additional qualitative comparisons in Appendix include the same initialized lift before and after correction, showing reduced scatter and more coherent motion with tracks and geometry held fixed. These comparisons complement the quantitative gains in Fig. 3. Videos are available on our project page. 4.4 ABLATION STUDY Simulated versus provider-generated lifts. We test whether training on provider-generated lifting errors transfers better than training on simulated corruptions. Both approaches use PointOdyssey with the same network and training budget  (Fig. 5)  . single simulated-lift model improves over the initialized lift on every dataset with both test geometry providers, outperforming models trained on AllTracker+DA3 or AllTracker+VGGT-Ω lifts. Both provider-trained models improve on their training scenes (+14.1 and +8.3 APD3D points for DA3 and VGGT-Ω, respectively), but these gains transfer inconsistently. DA3-lift training improves accuracy on held-out PointOdyssey scenes, but simulated training yields larger gains. The model trained on VGGT-Ω lifts reduces accuracy on every evaluated dataset. Provider-generated training requires aligning ground-truth targets, and discarding windows with unreliable alignment (Appendix D.1). To control for this selection, we repeat simulated-lift training on the same windows retained for DA3-lift training. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We showed that pretrained 2D tracks lifted with estimated geometry and simple gap initialization already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. Building on this observation, ReLift combines these providers with efficient feed-forward trajectory repair and completion for dense monocular 3D tracking. Training on simulated lifting errors enables one corrector to improve all evaluated trackergeometry combinations without retraining, with the largest gains on occluded points. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy on WorldTrack, while faster configurations retain competitive accuracy at substantially lower runtime than comparably accurate 3D trackers. Performance remains sensitive to input geometry (Appendix C.1), motivating future work on robustness to geometric and persistent correspondence errors.

We project 3D predictions through their associated cameras without groundtruth alignment. Projections are mapped to original image coordinates, accounting for resizing and crop offsets, before the common rescaling. Pointframes behind the ground-truth camera are excluded; predictions behind their camera or with non-finite projections count as misses at every threshold. Native AllTracker and CoWTracker predictions are scored directly in 2D at the same queries, with the same scaling and ground-truth masks. Track4World and DELTAv2 use inputs capped to our grid, with ADT uncapped (Appendix B.2). PS has identical All and Dyn scores because all its queries meet the dynamic-track criterion. Cameras for APD2D. Table 10 lists the projection cameras. Our method, TrackCraft3R and DELTAv2 use their geometry providers predicted intrinsics and extrinsics, following the shared estimated-geometry setup in Sec. 4.1. For methods without camera outputs, cameras are recovered from their own predictions without ground-truth camera parameters. Results. Native CoWTracker achieves the highest APD2D in every reported column, outperforming projected 3D trajectories and motivating our use of strong pretrained 2D correspondences (Sec. 4.2). Our CoWTracker variant with 4RC geometry leads mean All APD2D among 3D methods and ranks second on Dyn, behind Track4World. For either tracker, the means vary across geometry providers by only 0.15 (All) and at most 0.57 (Dyn) points. Tracker choice therefore has larger effect on APD2D here. 20 Relation to 3D accuracy. All six of our configurations remain below their native tracker in both means. With CoWTracker and 4RC geometry, the gaps are 1.48 points on All and 3.82 on Dyn. This comparison evaluates the complete pipeline; it neither isolates the correctors effect nor separates visible and occluded points. APD2D evaluates trajectories together with their projection cameras, including any camera recovery. It cannot measure range errors along valid viewing ray: lifting and reprojecting through the same camera returns the input pixel. The small variation across geometry providers therefore does not imply similar 3D accuracy. The APD3D gains over initialized lifts in Fig. 3 provide complementary evidence of improved 3D estimation.

sections.content: D.1 TRAINING ABLATION SETTINGS Simulated versus provider-generated lifts. Provider-generated lifts use AllTracker with DA3 or VGGT-Ω. To account for differences in coordinate frame and scale, we align ground-truth frame0 positions x0i to lifted positions y0i using similarity transform αRx0i + b. Valid points have positive frame-0 range. We first fit the transform by least squares on all valid points, then perform three refits to reduce the influence of outliers. After each fit, we compute the relative residual ei = αRx0i + y0i y0i . The next fitting set comprises valid points satisfying ei max(3 medianjKej, 0.01), where is the set used for the current fit. The 1% floor limits trimming when residuals are already low. After the final fit, we recompute the median residual over all valid points, including those excluded from fitting. We retain windows with at least 256 valid points, positive fitted scale, and finite median residual below 0.2. We apply this single transform to the ground truth at every frame, leaving the input lift unchanged. There is no per-frame refitting or additional alignment inside the loss, so errors in the estimated camera motion remain part of the correction task. After filtering, the runs trained on AllTracker+DA3 and AllTracker+VGGT-Ω lifts use 3,890 and 3,837 training windows, respectively. The latter must pass both providers filters. These models improve training-scene APD3D on all points by 14.14 and 8.33 percentage points over their corresponding lifts, respectively. We train an additional simulated-lift model on the same 3,890 filtered windows as the model trained on AllTracker+DA3 lifts, with the same architecture, optimization settings and 150,000 training steps. Figure 6 shows that simulated training still improves APD3D on every dataset and outperforms training on AllTracker+DA3 lifts with both test geometry providers.
